title: The Astronaut in Pajamas
summary: Vera's night light has broken and her room is very dark. That night, her bed turns into a rocket, and Vera flies all the way to the moon to look for a little light.

scenes.text:
That night, Vera's little lamp went plink! and went out.

It was a little lamp shaped like a mushroom, and it had been on every night since Vera was a baby.

"We'll buy a new one tomorrow," said Dad, and he kissed her forehead. "It's only one night."

But one night is a very long time when your room is dark.

Vera pulled the covers up to her nose and hugged Bruno, her teddy bear. The shadows of the wardrobe looked bigger than in the daytime. The chair looked like a man sitting down.

Only a little light came in through the window. It was the moon, curved like a smile above the rooftops.

"If only I had a tiny bit of that light…" Vera whispered.

Then the bed shook.

First it was a tiny tremble. Then a bigger one.

The legs of the bed folded inwards. The headboard stretched until it came to a point. Two colourful fins grew out of the sides, and underneath, a warm light began to hum.

Her bed had turned into a rocket.

Vera held on tight to the blanket. Bruno held on tight to Vera.

"Five, four, three, two, one…" she counted, barely making a sound.

And then… blastoff!

The bed flew out of the window, skimmed the rooftops and went up, up, up. Down below, the city grew tiny, its lit windows like crumbs of light. Up above, the sky was full of stars.

The bed landed gently on soft, silvery ground, like flour.

Vera put out one foot. Then the other. Her slippers left two round prints in the dust.

She was on the moon.

"Well, what a surprise," said a big, calm voice. "A little girl in pajamas. I haven't seen one of those in a long time."

It was the moon who was speaking. She had an enormous smile and half-closed eyes, like someone who has been awake all night.

"Sorry for coming without asking," said Vera. "It's just that my little lamp broke, and my room is very dark. Could you lend me a little light?"

The moon thought about it.

"I can't give you light, because I need it to light up the roads. But I know someone who might like to keep you company."

Behind a little hill of dust, all alone, there was a tiny star. So small it fit in the palm of a hand.

"She fell out of the sky a few days ago," said the moon. "And she's too little to climb back up on her own."

Vera picked her up very carefully. She was warm, like a mug of hot chocolate.

"Would you like to come to my house?" she asked. "You'll have a place of your own there."

The little star couldn't talk. But all of a sudden she sparkled, brighter than before. That meant yes.

Vera tucked her into her pajama pocket, said goodbye to the moon, and flew home in her rocket-bed, with Bruno peeking over the side.

Back in her room, Vera found the glass jar where she kept her buttons and tipped them out onto the rug.

She put the little star inside and set the jar on her bedside table.

What a beautiful light! Golden and soft, better than the little lamp's. The shadows of the wardrobe shrank. The chair went back to being a chair.

Vera snuggled down, happy.

But after a while she noticed something. The little star was shining less. And then a little less.

She wasn't looking at Vera. She wasn't looking at the room. She was looking out of the window, upwards, at the sky where all the others were.

Vera knew that face. It was the face she made on her first day of school, when Mum left.

"You miss your home," she said softly.

Vera got up, opened the window wide and took the lid off the jar.

"Go on," she said. "Go back to your family."

The little star floated out slowly. She circled once round Vera's head, like a hug, and began to rise. Higher than the rooftops. Higher than the clouds.

Until she found her place, right in front of Vera's window.

And from up there, she gave her a wink.

The room was dark again. But it was a different kind of dark now. It was a dark with someone looking in from outside.

Vera hugged Bruno, gave an enormous yawn and fell asleep.

The next day, Dad bought a new little lamp. But Vera hardly ever turns it on.
